echoes.note: The Holiness Code's demand for righteous, unbiased judgment ('you shall not be partial... but in righteousness shall you judge') underlies Jesus' critique of hypocritical, self-exempting judging.

Reproof of 'your brother/neighbor' without bearing sin or grudge frames the speck-and-beam logic: correction must be cleansed of self-righteousness; 'brother' language matches Lev's love-of-neighbor unit.
Nathan's 'You are the man!' — David condemns another's sin while blind to his own — is the narrative archetype of judging with a beam in one's eye.

Measure-for-measure principle ('with the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the crooked, shrewd'): God deals back in kind, echoed in 'with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.'
'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' — leaving recompense to God, the disposition behind 'judge not, that you be not judged.'
God judges with measured forbearance so the righteous learn to be kind; a Second Temple articulation of the reciprocal-measure ethic.
'Forgive your neighbor the wrong... and then your sins will be pardoned' — the reciprocity of judgment/forgiveness in wisdom tradition closely parallels 7:1-2.
'Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words' — withholding precious teaching from those who will only scorn it parallels not casting pearls before swine.
Correcting a scoffer brings abuse ('reprove a scoffer and he will hate you'); the rebuffing 'dogs' who 'turn and tear you' echoes the futility of instructing scorners.
A gold ring in a swine's snout — wisdom tradition's pairing of something precious with a pig as image of incongruity.
'That which is holy' (qodesh) — sacred offerings forbidden to the unconsecrated/profane — supplies cultic background for not giving the holy to dogs.
Sacred meat is to be thrown to the dogs as the antithesis of holy use; the dog as the unclean recipient of holy things underlies the saying's logic.
'You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart' — the seek/find promise behind 'Seek, and you will find.'
'From there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' — covenantal seek-and-find assurance.
Wisdom: 'those who seek me diligently find me' — the wisdom-tradition seek/find topos applied to prayer.
'Seek the LORD while he may be found, call upon him while he is near' — seeking and calling that meet divine availability.
'The LORD is near to all who call on him... he fulfills the desire of those who fear him' — the Father's reliable response to those who ask.
A mother cannot forget her nursing child — the a fortiori of parental compassion ('how much more your Father') has prophetic precedent.
'As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion' — the very father-to-children analogy of 7:11.
God hears the prayer of the wronged and does not ignore supplication — Second Temple confidence in answered petition.
'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — the Golden Rule reformulates the command Jesus elsewhere names as summing the Law (Mt 22:39-40), here explicitly 'the law and the prophets.'
'What you hate, do to no one' — the negative form of the Golden Rule in the deuterocanon; the closest verbal precedent to 7:12's reciprocity maxim.
Extension of neighbor-love to the resident alien ('love him as yourself') broadens the rule's scope to 'men' generally.
'Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own' — wisdom-tradition empathic reciprocity anticipating the Golden Rule.
The Mosaic 'two ways' — life and good vs. death and evil, with the call to 'choose life' — is the foundational template for the two gates/ways leading to life or destruction.
'I set before you the way of life and the way of death' — the explicit prophetic 'way of life / way of death' formula behind 7:13-14.
'The LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish' — the two-ways frame (the same Psalm informs 7:17-19 on trees/fruit).
The path of the righteous vs. the way of the wicked who stumble in darkness — wisdom's contrasted ways.
'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death' — the broad way that 'leads to destruction.'
'The way of sinners is smoothly paved... but at its end is the pit of Hades' — Second Temple two-ways with a broad/smooth road to destruction.
The blessing-and-curse alternative set before Israel reinforces the binary-choice structure.
Israel's princes are 'like wolves tearing the prey' for gain — the predatory-wolf image for corrupt leaders, here the false prophets 'inwardly ravening wolves.'
Judah's officials are 'roaring lions,' her judges 'evening wolves,' her prophets 'treacherous' — prophets/leaders as wolves cloaking treachery.
Warning against false prophets who speak from their own minds, not the LORD; the test of true vs. false prophecy frames 'beware of false prophets.'
The Torah test for a false prophet who leads astray though signs come true — background to discerning prophets 'by their fruits.'
The criterion for distinguishing the prophet who speaks presumptuously — judging the prophet by outcome/fruit.
The righteous as a tree yielding its fruit in season vs. the wicked as chaff — the good-tree/good-fruit and judgment imagery of Ps 1 underlies 7:17-19.
The one trusting the LORD is a tree by water that 'does not cease to bear fruit' — fruitfulness as the mark of right relation to God.
The vineyard yielding wild/bad grapes instead of good is judged and destroyed — bad fruit signaling false standing and impending judgment.
Ephraim 'blighted, their root dried up, they shall bear no fruit' — fruitlessness as ground for being cut off.
The coming day burns the evildoers like stubble; 'every tree that doesn't grow good fruit is... thrown into the fire' shares the burning-judgment image.
Trees whose fruit is for food, leaves for healing — the eschatological good-tree image as foil to the corrupt tree.
'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree, so the expression of a thought discloses the heart' — wisdom maxim that fruit reveals inner character.
'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' — verbatim source of Jesus' dismissal sentence in 7:23.
Prophets prophesy lies 'in my name' though the LORD did not send them — 'didn't we prophesy in your name?' echoes false prophecy claiming the divine name.
'They prophesy falsely in my name' — the divine repudiation of those who invoke God's name without commission.
'The LORD will make known who is his' — the motif of God knowing/owning his own, inverted in 'I never knew you.'
'The LORD knows the way of the righteous' — divine 'knowing' as covenantal acknowledgment, denied to the iniquitous in 7:23.
Israel cries 'My God, we know you!' yet has spurned the good — claiming acquaintance with God while doing iniquity, repudiated.
'When the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever' — the storm that sweeps away the unfounded vs. the firmly founded, the core contrast of the two builders.
'The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand' — the standing vs. falling house image.

False prophets build a wall and daub it with whitewash; rain, hailstones and wind break it down so it falls — the rain/flood/wind destroying a poorly founded structure, directly behind the collapsing house. (Links the false-prophet warning of 7:15 to its judgment.)
God lays a tested foundation stone; hail sweeps away the refuge of lies, waters overflow the shelter — the secure foundation vs. the false refuge swept by flood.
Hearing-and-doing vs. hearing-only mirrors the righteous (rooted, enduring) vs. the wicked (chaff driven away, not standing in judgment).
Doing the words of the covenant yields life and stability — the hear-and-do framing of blessing/endurance.
The godless one's confidence is a spider's web; he leans on his house and it does not stand — the collapsing house of the one without firm trust.
'By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established' — the wise builder whose house stands.
Those who hear God's words but do not do them — hearing without doing, the foolish builder's failing.

The promised prophet like Moses in whose mouth God puts his words — Jesus teaching 'with authority, not like the scribes' presents him as that authoritative prophetic voice, fitting Matthew's new-Moses framing of the Sermon.
The people's awe at the words spoken from Sinai parallels the multitudes 'astonished at his teaching' on the mountain.
The people respond as Moses delivers the LORD's words; the crowd's reaction frames Jesus' Sermon as a covenant-law delivery from the mount.
